title: Authority Isn't Power
author: Scott D. Clary
summary: Clary distinguishes between authority and power in organizations. Authority is visible on the org chart, the ability to make decisions. Power is invisible until you need it, the ability to determine which decisions get made. An executive assistant decides which decisions reach the CEO's desk, which means the assistant often has more power than people realize. A person who spent eighteen months trying to reach a CEO through cold outreach and LinkedIn will get nowhere; someone who cultivates a relationship with the CEO's assistant gets a meeting in two weeks. Most people miss this dynamic because power isn't visible on the org chart and doesn't match our assumptions about hierarchy. Understanding where power actually resides unlocks influence.
points: Authority is the ability to make decisions and is visible on the org chart; power is the ability to determine which decisions get made and is invisible until you need it.
An executive assistant often holds more practical power than most middle managers because they control access and information flow to decision makers.

Spending eighteen months trying to reach someone through cold outreach and formal channels can fail entirely, while building a relationship with that person's assistant can yield results in two weeks.
Most people cannot tell the difference between authority and power because power is not listed on the org chart and contradicts conventional hierarchical assumptions.
Understanding where power actually lives in an organization requires observation and relationship-building rather than relying on formal structure or titles.
quotes: The CEO has authority. The executive assistant has power. Most people can't tell the difference.
Authority is the ability to make decisions. Power is the ability to determine which decisions get made. Authority is visible on the org chart. Power is invisible until you need it.

You spend eighteen months trying to reach a CEO you want to partner with. Cold emails. LinkedIn messages. Mutual connections. Zero response. Your colleague gets a meeting with the same person in two weeks.
You ask how. I called and talked to his assistant. We ended up chatting about her son's soccer team for a few minutes. She asked what I needed. I explained. She found a time.
You think your colleague got lucky. Your colleague understood where power actually lives.” Archived from newsletter.scottdclary.com on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
